summary: This informational document describes use cases for telepresence systems that give separated users a feeling of co-located presence through high-fidelity audio and video. It looks at the stream-handling techniques they use.

plainLanguage.summary: A telepresence room has several cameras and several screens, arranged so that people at the far end look as if they were sitting across the table. There is no agreed way to say which camera belongs to which screen or which audio stream belongs to which person. This RFC lists the situations a standard would have to cover.

questions: how do telepresence systems handle multiple cameras
subtitle: Scenarios that show why telepresence rooms need a common way to describe their many streams.

tldr.problem: Telepresence rooms use several cameras, several screens and several audio streams so that remote participants appear life-size across the table. Different vendors implement the same idea differently, and making two systems talk needs translation equipment that adds delay.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes eight typical scenarios from the user's point of view: symmetric and asymmetric point-to-point meetings, multipoint meetings, presentation streams, mixed endpoint types, a classroom, a virtual space, and a surgical consultation. It lists the parameters that describe a room and shows what each scenario does with them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that defines no protocol. It is a set of use cases from which requirements are to be derived in a separate document, so that a future standard can say what each stream in a conference is for.

facts.label: Asymmetric example
facts.value: 3 screens at one site, 1 at the other

facts.label: People at the table in that example
facts.value: Up to 2 at the 1-screen room, up to 6 at the 3-screen room

today: RFC 7205 is an Informational RFC published in April 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a set of use cases from which a later requirements document was to be derived.

sections.title: Why Telepresence Needs a Common Description
sections.content:
Telepresence applications try to give a being there experience for conversational video conferencing. It is often called immersive telepresence, to distinguish it from traditional video conferencing and from other forms of remote presence such as avatars and robots. The characteristics that mark it out are usually described as being actual sized, providing immersive video, preserving interpersonal interaction, and allowing non-verbal communication.

Although telepresence systems are built on open standards such as RTP, SIP, H.264 and the H.323 suite of protocols, they cannot easily interoperate with each other without operator assistance and expensive extra equipment that translates from one vendor's protocol to another. The features that give telepresence its distinctive character are implemented in disparate ways in different systems. Systems from diverse vendors do interoperate to some extent today, but not in a standards-based way, and interworking requires translation and transcoding devices in the architecture.

Those devices increase latency, which reduces the quality of the interaction between people. Using them is also often not automatic: it frequently needs substantial manual configuration and a detailed understanding of the underlying audio and video streams. The RFC calls that state of affairs unacceptable for the continued growth of telepresence, and argues that these systems should have the same ease of interoperability as telephones. A standard way of describing the multiple streams that make up the media flows, and the fundamental aspects of their behaviour, would let telepresence systems interwork.

The document itself is a set of use cases. Requirements are to be derived from them in a separate document, and the use cases are written from the viewpoint of the users. They illustrate the user experience that has to be supported, and it is possible to implement them in a variety of ways.
sections.plainLanguage: Two telepresence rooms from different makers cannot simply talk to each other. Making them talk needs a translator box, and the box adds delay to a conversation that depends on quick reactions.

sections.title: The Building Blocks of a Room
sections.content:
A telepresence system is typically composed of one or more video cameras and encoders and one or more display screens of large size, with a diagonal around 60 inches. Microphones pick up sound, and the audio codecs produce one or more audio streams. The cameras used to capture the users are called participant cameras, and likewise for the screens. There may also be other cameras, such as a document camera; these are called presentation cameras or content cameras, and they generally have different formats, aspect ratios and frame rates from the participant cameras. The presentation streams may be shown on participant screens or on auxiliary display screens. A user's computer may also serve as a virtual content camera, generating an animation or playing a video for the remote participants.

The RFC lists thirteen parameters that describe a typical scenario: the number of participating sites; the number of visible seats at a site; the number of cameras; the number and type of microphones; the number of audio channels; the screen size; the screen capabilities such as resolution, frame rate and aspect ratio; the arrangement of the screens in relation to each other; the number of primary screens at each site; the type and number of presentation screens; the multipoint conference display strategies, for example whether the camera-to-screen mappings are static or dynamic; the camera point of capture; and the fields of view of the cameras and how they relate spatially to each other.

The problem the RFC names is that there is no agreed way to describe the semantics of how streams of various media types relate to each other. Without a standard for stream semantics describing the particular role and activity of each stream in the conference, interoperability is cumbersome at best. In a multiple-screen conference the incoming streams must be understood so that they can be presented in a coherent and life-like manner: remote participants shown at their actual size for their apparent distance, correct eye contact, gesticular cues, and a spatial audio sound stage consistent with the displayed video.

The receiving device that decides how to render incoming information needs to know the spatial position of the speaker, the field of view of the cameras, the camera zoom, and which media stream relates to each of the screens. It is not simply that individual streams must be described adequately, since that largely exists already, but that the semantics of the relationships between the streams must be communicated. This is needed even when the basic aspects of the streams, such as bit rate, frame rate and aspect ratio, are known.
sections.plainLanguage: A room has cameras for people and separate cameras for slides, and each screen is paired with one camera. The receiving end has to know which camera goes with which screen and where each speaker is sitting, or it cannot line the picture up with the sound.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Meetings
sections.content:
In the symmetric case each of the two sites has an identical number of screens, cameras with fixed fields of view, and one camera for each screen, and the sound type is the same at both ends. The example given is three cameras and three screens in each room, with stereo sound sent and received at each end. Each screen is paired with a corresponding camera, and each pair is typically connected to a separate codec, producing an encoded stream for transmission and receiving a similarly encoded stream from the far end.

Each system has one or more microphones for capturing audio. Stereophonic microphones may be used, or a microphone may sit in front of each participant or pair of participants, and in typical systems all the microphones are connected to a single codec that sends and receives the audio streams as stereo or surround sound. The number of microphones and the number of audio channels are often not the same as the number of cameras, and the number of microphones is often not the same as the number of loudspeakers. Audio levels should be matched so that the sound levels at both sites are identical.

The loudspeaker and microphone placements are chosen so that the sound stage, the orientation of the apparent audio sources, is coordinated with the video. If a participant at one site speaks, the participants at the remote site hear her voice coming from her image, which means the audio has to be mapped at the receiving site in the same fashion as the video: audio received from the right side of the room has to come out of the loudspeakers on the left at the remote site, and the other way round. The same left and right relationship drives the video, since the left side of each room is presented on the right screen at the far end, so that participants at each site appear to be sitting across the table from each other.

In the asymmetric case the two sites have different numbers of screens and cameras, which different systems handle in different ways. The example takes three screens and three cameras at one site and one screen and one camera at the other, with the screen sizes and camera fields of view similar, so that each camera view is designed to show two people sitting side by side. The one-screen room then seats up to two people and the three-screen room up to six. Defining left and right and indicating the relative placement of the multiple audio and video streams works as in the symmetric case, but the mismatch has to be handled. Four approaches are described: show one of the three streams on the single screen, which shows two people at full size but hides the other four, and the choice of stream can be fixed, made by the users, or made automatically from who is speaking, in which case the sender can suppress the streams that are not displayed; receive and decode all three streams and compose them into one local image, which shows all six but smaller than full size and can be paired with reducing the resolution so that resources are not wasted on streams that will be downsized anyway; have the three-screen side include all six people in a single stream, either by physically adjusting pan, tilt and zoom cameras so one camera covers the whole room or by recomposing the three camera images into one encoded stream, which again shows all six at reduced size; or a combination, showing the speaker at full size alongside a composite of all six at a smaller size. The receiving system needs to know the content of the streams it receives to make any of these decisions, and if both systems support more than one strategy they need to negotiate which one to use.
sections.plainLanguage: In a two-room call each camera has a matching screen and the audio is swapped left for right so the sound comes from the picture. When the rooms have different numbers of screens, one side has to pick, crop or combine the pictures, and the two sides have to agree which way.

sections.title: Multipoint Meetings
sections.content:
In a multipoint conference more than two sites take part, and extra complexity is needed so that the streams from each participant appear on the other participants' screens. There are many topologies for displaying the streams from multiple sites. One major objective of telepresence is to preserve the being there experience, but in multi-site conferences it is often not possible at the same time to provide full-size video, eye contact, and a common perception of gestures and gaze. Several distribution and display policies exist, and all give good results while making different compromises.

Site switching forwards all the camera images from the site where the speaker is to every other site, so all the screens at each remote site show that one site. This preserves full-size images and the full visual context of the displayed far end. The relation between the cameras in each room and the screens in remote rooms is fixed, and the room or participants being shown are switched from time to time, based on who is speaking or by manual control.

Segment switching shows only the speaker at the active site rather than all of that site's images. The camera images of the current speaker and of previous speakers, if any, are forwarded to the other sites, so the screens at each site usually show images from different remote sites. This preserves full-size images and also captures the non-verbal communication between speakers, and the display depends on the activity in the remote rooms, generally but not necessarily on speech detection.

The third possibility is to reduce the image size so that multiple camera views can be composited onto one or more screens. That does not preserve full-size display but gives the most visual context, since more sites or segments can be seen, and the display mapping is typically static, with each part of each room shown in the same place throughout the conference. Other policies and combinations are possible, such as a static display of all screens from all remote rooms with part of one screen used to show the current speaker at full size.
sections.plainLanguage: With more than two rooms you cannot show everyone at full size. The three ways out are to show one whole room, to show one person at a time, or to shrink everybody into a picture on one screen.

sections.title: Presentation Streams
sections.content:
Besides the video and audio streams showing the participants, additional streams are used for presentations. In systems available today generally only one additional video stream is available for presentations, and it is often half-duplex in nature, with presenters taking turns. The presentation stream may be captured from a PC screen or may come from a multimedia source such as a document camera, a camcorder or a DVD. In a multipoint meeting the presentation streams for the active presentation are always distributed to all sites so that everyone sees them.

Some systems display the presentation stream on a screen mounted above or below the participant screens, while others provide screens on the conference table. Where several presentation screens are used, they generally show identical content, and there is considerable variation in the placement, number and size of them. In some systems the presentation audio is pre-mixed with the room audio, while in others a separate presentation audio stream is provided if the presentation includes audio. In H.323 systems the H.239 mechanism is typically used to control the video presentation stream, and in SIP systems similar control can be provided with the Binary Floor Control Protocol for the presentation token. Those mechanisms suit a single presentation stream.

Although today's systems remain limited to one video presentation stream, the RFC gives three obvious uses for more than one. The meeting convener may be following an agenda and want to show it to everybody while other participants take turns presenting, with the agenda and the presentation shown together on separate screens or rescaled onto one. A single multimedia presentation may itself contain several video streams that should be shown together, such as slides supporting a presenter's conclusions together with video excerpts from news programmes played from a DVD so that they can be paused and repositioned. And an educator presenting a multiscreen slide show needs the placement of the images on the multiple screens at each site to be consistent.

The telemedicine use case shows what several presentation streams are for. The local site is a surgery room connected to one or more remote sites that may have different capabilities. Three main cameras capture the whole room, in the usual three-camera telepresence arrangement, and multiple presentation inputs are available: a surgery camera giving a zoomed view of the operation, an endoscopic monitor, a fluoroscope, an ultrasound diagnostic device and an electrocardiogram monitor. These give several local video presentation streams that help the surgeon monitor the patient and assist in the procedure.

The local site may have three main screens and one or more presentation screens. The main screens show the remote experts, and the presentation screens show several presentation streams from local and remote sites at once. The surgeon decides the number, size and placement of the presentations on the local presentation screens, and indicates which local captures are provided to the remote sites; the local site can send several captures out and receive several presentations relating to the patient or the procedure. One kind of remote site is a single or dual screen and one camera system used by a consulting expert, and the remote sites can also be part of a multipoint conference. Their presentation screens let the experts see the details of the operation and the related data, and the experts can decide the number, size and placement of the presentations shown, and can themselves start sending presentation streams carrying medical records, pathology data, or their references and analysis. Another kind of remote site is a typical immersive room with three camera and screen pairs, letting more experts join, and these sites can also be used for education, with the teacher and the students in different remote sites, observing and learning the details of the whole procedure while the teacher explains and answers questions. Multiple presentation screens can be used across all of these sites to enhance visibility, one screen for the zoomed surgery stream and the others for medical image streams such as MRI images, cardiograms, ultrasonic images and pathology data.
sections.plainLanguage: Presentations are a separate stream from the people, and today a room usually has room for only one. Several streams would let a chair show an agenda beside a presentation, or a surgeon send a zoomed view of an operation along with scans and test results.

sections.title: Mixed Systems, Classrooms and Virtual Space
sections.content:
People often join a meeting from a variety of environments using different endpoint devices. A multiscreen immersive conference may include someone on a PC-based video conferencing system, a participant calling in by phone and someone on a handheld device. Some devices can handle multiple streams and others only one, and in a single-stream device the stream may contain one or more compositions depending on the screen space available. In most cases an intermediate transcoding device is relied on to produce a single stream, perhaps with some form of continuous presence. Bit rates vary, with the handheld device and phone lower than PC and multiscreen systems.

Layout follows different policies. A handheld device and a PC may receive the active speaker stream, and the decision can be made by the receiver or by the sender if it can receive a rendering hint. The same applies to audio: a mixed stream, or the loudest speakers if mixing is not available in the network. The PC participant's experience depends on the application, which might give a single stream like a handheld device but on a bigger screen, or multiple streams like an immersive system but on a smaller one, with stream control either local to the software or somewhere else and sent over the network. The handheld device is the most extreme case: it should be an equal participant even though its bandwidth is much lower, and a receiver may choose to display its output differently because of its resolution, which would equally apply to any low-resolution stream. It sends and receives a single video stream, which could be a composite or a subset of the conference, and it can either say what it wants or accept whatever the sender thinks is best, and it has to signal any actions it wants to take the same way an immersive system does.

The education use case is different, because the multiple video streams are not used to build a panoramic view at all. Instead they are used dynamically so that remote students can take part fully. The main site is a university auditorium with three cameras: one on the professor at the podium, one on the wall behind her capturing the class, and one co-located with the second that captures a close-up of a questioner and automatically zooms in on that student using sound localisation. The auditorium has only two screens, one large at the front for the class and one at the rear for the professor. When someone asks a question the front screen shows the questioner and otherwise the professor. The remote sites are typical immersive rooms with three camera and screen pairs; all of them show the professor on the centre screen at full size, and the second screen shows the whole classroom view when the professor is speaking, but a close-up of the student at full size when a student asks a question. The remote systems never display the students actually in that room. A question from a remote site appears on the auditorium screen at full size, as if the person were present, and on the rear screen so the professor can respond without turning her back on the class. When nobody is asking a question the rear screen briefly shows a full-room view of each remote site in turn, and the professor can also pick a particular site from a control on the podium. Realising this needs no negotiation between the sites: the endpoints, and the Multipoint Control Unit if there is one, need to know who is speaking and which video stream contains that speaker, and the auditorium system needs to know what sites are available so that it can request a view of any of them. Bandwidth is optimised if video that is not being shown at a site is not distributed to it.

The virtual space case puts every participant in a shared virtual room, each with a fixed seat, so each participant expects to see a different view with a different person on either side. The idea was proposed in 1983 and is implemented in several products today; the main difference from 1983 is the size of the screens. It assumes endpoints with multiple cameras and screens, usually the same number of each, with a camera positioned above each screen. The key detail is how the cameras are aimed: they are each aimed at the same area of view of the participants at the site, so each camera takes a picture of the same set of people from a different angle. A camera above the screen to a participant's left may take a picture of that participant's left ear, and one above the screen to the right a picture of the right ear. Each sender therefore offers a choice of streams, and an association is made between the receiving stream output on a particular screen and the corresponding sending stream from the camera above that screen, repeated for each pair in the meeting. The result is a horizontal arrangement of images from remote sites, one per screen, with excellent eye contact.
sections.plainLanguage: The same streams have to work when a phone joins a three-screen room, when a classroom sends a close-up of a student to distant lecture theatres, and when every participant sits in one shared virtual room with a camera above every screen.

viz.caption: PARAMETERS THAT DESCRIBE A TELEPRESENCE ROOM

items.title: Sites and seats
items.text: How many sites take part, and how many people are visible at each one.

items.title: Cameras
items.text: How many, and where they point. Participant cameras and presentation cameras differ in format and frame rate.

items.title: Microphones
items.text: How many and of what type. Often more microphones than audio channels or loudspeakers.

items.title: Audio channels
items.text: How many audio streams the codecs produce, and whether they are mixed.

items.title: Screens
items.text: Their size, resolution, frame rate and aspect ratio, and how they are arranged relative to each other.

items.title: Display strategy
items.text: How cameras are mapped to screens, and whether that mapping is fixed or changes during the call.
